scorecard.rationale: Two randomized human controlled trials report reduced acute procedural pain with topical clove preparations: a split-mouth placebo-controlled trial in 73 adults found glycerin gel prepared with ground clove lowered dental needle-insertion pain versus placebo (PMID16530911, p=.005), and a double-blind crossover in 34 hemodialysis patients found topical eugenol nanoemulsion lowered cannulation puncture pain versus no intervention and placebo gel (PMID32951708, p=.001; placebo mean omitted from public abstract). Competing studies show inconclusive three-arm postoperative headache contrasts for inhaled clove aromatherapy (PMID40012817, p=.20 at 8 h and p=.31 at 24 h), an unquantified null mouse hot-water report for ground clove powder (CCRAS 1997-1998), and assay-dependent rat essential-oil nanogel formalin versus hot-plate results (PMC9123718). Topical procedural versus oral chronic Parkinson pain and competing null trials keep the easing signal at minimal_signal. The clove entry in the 2016 natural-product screen measures cellular endpoints after extract exposure. This adds preparation context without an observed change in pain severity. The original randomized trial adds potentially contrary context. A powdered mixture including cloves and multiple other botanicals had six abdominal-pain reports in 32 participants versus two of 32 with placebo. It measured adverse-event occurrence in constipation care, without a clove-only group, severity, or a Parkinson population. The net lean continues to rest on the existing topical acute-pain contrasts, with limited transfer. The cardiac review identifies eugenol as a clove-oil constituent. Its cited cardiac and sensory mechanisms add no ground clove pain-severity contrast and do not change the earlier mixed oral and topical evidence.
